hints: Look closely at the word monoclonal and remember which part of a Y-shaped antibody actually touches the antigen.
Recall the two jobs: variable region binds antigen, constant region binds phagocyte receptors, and think what happens when those two parts are no longer joined together.
walkthrough:
**Recall antibody structure**

Think of an antibody like a Y shape with two functional ends. The tips of the arms are the variable regions and they form the antigen-binding sites. The stem is the constant region and it never binds antigen, it binds to receptors on phagocytes.

Rule: variable binds antigen, constant binds phagocyte.

**Use the word monoclonal**

Monoclonal means all the antibodies are identical copies from one clone of B cells. So every variable region has exactly the same shape and binds exactly the same epitope (the same part) of the virus antigen. This makes statement 3 true and statement 1 false.

**Check phagocytosis after separation**

For opsonisation, the antibody must act as a bridge: variable end holds the virus, constant end is grabbed by the phagocyte. Here the enzyme has cut that bridge. Free variable fragments can still bind virus but have no tail for phagocytes to grab, and free constant fragments have nothing to hold onto. So engulfment cannot be triggered, statement 2 is false. Only 3 is correct, so answer D.

options.A: Incorrect because 1 is false (constant regions do not bind antigen) and 2 is false (separated fragments cannot bridge virus to phagocyte).
options.B: Incorrect because although 3 is true, 1 is false since it is the variable, not constant, region that binds antigen.
options.C: Incorrect because 2 is false, phagocytosis needs intact antibody to link virus to phagocyte, which is lost after enzyme treatment.
options.D: Correct because only 3 is true, all monoclonal variable regions are identical and bind the same epitope on the virus antigen.
